rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer:
You choose the order. Timestamps don't come into it. **Walking Ballista** enters with either **6** or **5** +1/+1 counters, depending on which effect you apply first, so pick Scales first to get 6.

Ballista's "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" puts 2 counters on it. **Hardened Scales** and **Doubling Season** are both replacement effects that modify that event. When two or more replacement effects apply, the affected object's controller (you) chooses one to apply, then the process repeats with whatever still applies (`616.1`, `616.1f`). Neither is a self-replacement effect or a control/copy/back-face effect, so you can freely choose either one (`616.1e`). The Scryfall ruling on Hardened Scales says the same: you choose the order, no matter who controls the sources.

The two orders:
- Scales first: 2 becomes 3, then Doubling Season makes it **6**.
- Doubling Season first: 2 becomes 4, then Scales makes it **5**.

Each effect applies only once to the event (`614.5`). Both effects do work on counters a permanent enters with, per the rulings for each card.
citations: rule 616.1: "the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."

rule 616.1f: "Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply."

ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."
rule 614.5: "A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event."
ruling 01546b7d-a233-4176-8843-d732074dc5b6/30e1af27509ea83b: "Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No. While **Blood Moon** is out, your Tron lands are just Mountains. Each one taps for {R} only, so you get 3 red mana, not 7 colorless.

Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That sets each Urza land's subtype to Mountain. Per `305.7`, the land then "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types," and gains the mana ability of its new basic land type. So **Urza's Tower** loses its whole printed ability, including the "add {C}{C}{C} instead" part. It gets "{T}: Add {R}" in its place.

The lands also stop being Urza's Tower, Urza's Mine and Urza's Power-Plant by type. The Tron abilities check land types, not names. So even if one of those abilities somehow survived, it couldn't find the other two. The cards keep their names, and they stay nonbasic (`305.8`), but that doesn't help you.

As soon as Blood Moon leaves the battlefield, they're normal Tron lands again.
citations: oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."

rule 305.7: "It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type."

ruling 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae/de7b24c7cfc8d0d2: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability \"{T}: Add {R}.\""
ruling 32fbb638-ab14-4e8b-a07a-d4c44e3496f2/67514ffa8ee40389: "The ability checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control."
rule 305.8: "Any land that doesn’t have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type."

rows.question: follow up: what if I play [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] AFTER the moon is already down? urborg has the later timestamp so shouldn't it make everything a Swamp too? my friend says no
rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's (613.8a): applying Blood Moon makes Urborg a Mountain and strips its rules-text ability (305.7), which removes the existence of Urborg's effect. When a dependency exists it overrides timestamps (613.8), so Blood Moon applies first no matter which entered later (613.8b). Urborg is just a Mountain with '{T}: Add {R}' and nothing becomes a Swamp. (Any actual basic Swamps you control are still Swamps because Blood Moon only affects nonbasic lands.)

outcome.answer:
Your friend is right. Even with the later timestamp, **Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth** makes nothing a Swamp while **Blood Moon** is on the battlefield. Urborg is just a legendary Mountain that taps for {R}.

Why: Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" and Urborg's "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types" are both type-changing effects in layer 4. Timestamps normally decide the order within a layer, but dependency overrides them (`613.8`). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's, because applying Blood Moon changes whether Urborg's effect exists at all (`613.8a`). Blood Moon sets Urborg's subtype to Mountain, so per `305.7` Urborg "loses all abilities generated from its rules text." The dependent effect waits until Blood Moon has applied (`613.8b`). By then Urborg no longer has the ability, so its effect never applies.

The Urborg ruling confirms this for an effect like Magus of the Moon, which works the same way as Blood Moon: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply." Urborg does stay legendary, and your basic lands keep their normal types. They just don't become Swamps.
citations: rule 613.8a: "applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to"
rule 613.8b: "An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied."
rule 305.7: "If an effect sets a land’s subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text"
ruling db6174d7-211d-4817-b8e4-8384594c83f9/aebb4d57471c5c28: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."
oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."

rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer:
Their Clone is just a regular **Tarmogoyf**. It gets none of your counters and none of the **Giant Growth** boost, but it does get the ability that sets Goyf's power and toughness, so it works out its own size.

Per `707.2`, a copy takes only the copiable values, meaning what's printed on the card. "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied." So your two +1/+1 counters stay with your Goyf, and so does the +3/+3 from Giant Growth, which is a non-copy effect. The Clone ruling says the same: it doesn't copy counters or "any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness".

As for the */*+1: Tarmogoyf's printed text is an ability, and per `707.2a` "A copy acquires the abilities of the object it’s copying because those values are derived from its rules text." So the Clone has "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1" and counts the graveyards itself. Its base power and toughness always match your Goyf's base. Your Goyf is simply +5/+5 bigger (+2/+2 from counters, +3/+3 from Giant Growth) until end of turn, when the Growth wears off. After that, only the counters keep it bigger.

One side effect: Giant Growth goes to the graveyard once it resolves. If it's the first instant in any graveyard, it pumps both Goyfs by +1/+1 through the ability.
citations: rule 707.2: "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied."
rule 707.2a: "A copy acquires the abilities of the object it’s copying because those values are derived from its rules text."

ruling 42226b87-0746-4ebf-9fd0-108d508462af/e115f2763b5d5e7e: "It doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it, or any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness"
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

outcome.answer:
Your other creatures are still 1/1 with no abilities either way. **Opalescence** is never a creature, because it "Each other non-Aura enchantment" leaves Opalescence itself out. **Humility**'s size is the only thing that depends on timestamps.

**Humility out first, Opalescence enters later (your case):**
- Layer 4: Opalescence turns Humility into an enchantment creature.
- Layer 6: Humility is now a creature, so it loses all abilities, including its own. Per `613.6`, an effect that has started applying keeps applying in its other layers "even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process." So Humility's effect still applies in layer 7b.
- Layer 7b: Both effects set base P/T, so they apply in timestamp order (`613.4b`, `613.7`). A permanent gets its timestamp when it enters (`613.7d`). Humility makes every creature 1/1 first. Then Opalescence makes Humility 4/4, because its mana value is 4.

Result: Humility is a 4/4 enchantment creature with no abilities. Your other creatures are 1/1 with no abilities. Opalescence is a normal enchantment and keeps its ability.

**Opalescence out first:** The layers work the same way, but in 7b Opalescence makes Humility 4/4 first. Then Humility's later effect makes it 1/1. So Humility is 1/1 with no abilities, and everything else is still 1/1. The official Scryfall ruling on these two cards walks through both orders the same way.

Any other non-Aura enchantments on the battlefield also become creatures, and they lose their abilities too. Their size follows the same timestamp logic. If Humility was there first, they get P/T equal to their mana value. If Opalescence was there first, they're 1/1.
citations: rule 613.6: "If an effect starts to apply in one layer and/or sublayer, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the …"
rule 613.4b: "Layer 7b: Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied. Effects that refer to the base power and/or toughness of a creature apply in this layer."
rule 613.7: "An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp."
rule 613.7d: "An object receives a timestamp at the time it enters a zone."
ruling ed7bdb3e-5c51-4547-9266-76a791e0b2b0/18649cad787b2eba: "Layer 7b: Humility becomes 1/1 and Worship becomes 1/1 (Humility). Humility becomes 4/4 and Worship becomes 4/4 (Opalescence)."
oracle 59489b46-9d02-4f3c-bcd0-884e7605e9a5#0: "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value."

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes. You can cast **Valki, God of Lies** as **Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** for {5}{B}{R}. In your library or graveyard, though, it is only a Valki creature card, not a planeswalker card.

**Casting:** Per `712.11b`, when you cast a modal double-faced card you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack. The spell has only the characteristics of that face (`712.8f`), and it enters the battlefield as Tibalt, a planeswalker.

**Other zones:** Per `712.8a`, anywhere other than the battlefield or the stack, the card has only its front face's characteristics. In your library, graveyard, hand or exile it is a Legendary Creature — God with mana value 2. It is not a planeswalker card and not mana value 7.

For your two examples: **Vraska's Contempt** and **Kaya's Ghostform** only care about permanents on the battlefield. A Tibalt you've cast is a planeswalker there, so Contempt can exile it and Ghostform can enchant it. One catch with Ghostform: if Tibalt dies or is exiled, Ghostform returns "that card" to the battlefield. A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from anywhere except the stack enters front face up (`712.14`), so it comes back as Valki, not Tibalt. Valki's enter trigger will then make each opponent reveal their hand again.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."
rule 712.14: "A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default."
oracle b15c6203-6311-44eb-916d-a4c271960c74#0: "When enchanted permanent dies or is put into exile, return that card to the battlefield under your control."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right on the first point. You're right on the second: a "counter target creature spell" effect can't touch **Stomp**.

**Casting from exile:** When an Adventure spell resolves, you exile it instead of putting it in your graveyard. Per `715.3d`, "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can't be cast as an Adventure this way." So you can cast **Bonecrusher Giant** from exile, but not Stomp again. Normal timing still applies, so that's usually your main phase with an empty stack. The exception is another effect that separately lets you cast it as an Adventure, which `715.3d` allows for.

**Countering:** While Stomp is on the stack as an Adventure, it has only its Adventure characteristics (`715.3b`). The ruling puts it this way: "use the alternative characteristics and ignore all of the card's normal characteristics." That makes Stomp a red instant spell with mana value 2, not a creature spell. A "counter target creature spell" effect can't target it. A plain "counter target spell" could. If Stomp is countered that way, the card goes to your graveyard instead of exile, and you lose the option to cast the Giant later.
citations: rule 715.3d: "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way, although other effects that allow a player to cast it may allow a player to cast it as an A…"
rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."
ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/700df45a4e7078ff: "use the alternative characteristics and ignore all of the card's normal characteristics"

ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/9f9546560bbab6ce: "If an Adventure spell leaves the stack in any way other than resolving (most likely by being countered or by failing to resolve because its targets have all become illegal), that card won't be exiled"

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, the
search happens once and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile. It is Brisela's controller who
searches, not the player who cast Path to Exile ("Its controller may search their library
for a basic land card"), and any basic land will do, not only a Plains.

outcome.answer:
Neither of your guesses: **Blood Artist** doesn't trigger at all, and you get one basic land from **Path to Exile**.

**Blood Artist:** it triggers "Whenever this creature or another creature dies." A creature dies only when it goes to the graveyard. Path exiles **Brisela**, so nothing died and nothing triggers. If Brisela had died instead, it would still count once, not twice. Per `712.21e`, a melded permanent counts as one object that moved. It counts as two only when an effect cares about the number of *cards*. When a melded permanent leaves, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards go to the new zone (`712.21`). So both **Bruna** and **Gisela** end up in exile.

**Path:** it exiles one target creature (Brisela is one creature). Then "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped." That's a single search for one card. Also, it doesn't have to be a Plains: you can pick any basic land card.
citations: rule 712.21e: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved."
rule 712.21: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."
oracle d683d985-9888-4d21-8b5f-69e69ce4a03b#0: "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle."

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

outcome.answer:
No, that trick doesn't work anymore. **Waylay** has Oracle errata. Its current text reads "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step." Cards printed with "at end of turn" got updated Oracle wording (`513.1a`), and Waylay's exile was moved to the cleanup step specifically to shut down this play.

If you cast it during your opponent's end step, the next cleanup step is the very next step of that same turn: "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup" (`512.1`). When that cleanup step starts, the game checks for any triggered abilities waiting to go on the stack, "including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”". The exile trigger goes on the stack, players get priority, it resolves and the Knights are exiled. Then another cleanup step begins (`514.3a`).

So the Knights only last for the rest of your opponent's end step. They can still work as surprise blockers if you cast Waylay earlier in combat, or as sacrifice fodder, but they never make it to your turn.

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
No. **Lion's Eye Diamond** is a mana ability, but it can only be activated when you have priority. That rules out using it to pay for **Infernal Tutor** in the middle of casting it.

Your Mirage card's wording doesn't count. Per `108.1`, the card does what its current Oracle text says: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant." The ability is still a mana ability, whatever timing restriction it has (`605.1`). Normally, mana abilities can be activated in the middle of casting a spell (`605.3a`). But "Activate only as an instant" means you follow the timing rules for casting an instant (`602.5e`). You can cast an instant only when you have priority (`117.1a`), and you don't get priority partway through casting a spell. The Scryfall ruling says the same: it resolves as a mana ability, "but it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant."

You don't need that trick anyway. As soon as you start casting Tutor, it moves from your hand to the stack (`601.2a`), so it would never be discarded. The usual line is to pay for Tutor with other mana, hold priority, and crack LED with Tutor on the stack. Your hand gets discarded, you get three mana, and Tutor resolves with hellbent active: "If you have no cards in hand, instead search your library for a card."
citations: rule 108.1: "Use the Oracle card reference when determining a card’s wording."

rule 117.1a: "A player may cast an instant spell any time they have priority."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer:
You drain for all of them, Blood Artist included. When **Wrath of God** destroys everything at once, **Blood Artist** triggers once for each creature that died, itself too.

**Blood Artist** says "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life." A creature dying is a leaves-the-battlefield trigger. Per `603.10a`, those triggers "look back in time": the game checks the moment just before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield. So it sees every creature dying alongside it. The example under `603.10` covers this exact situation: an artifact destroyed together with two creatures still triggers twice.

Per `603.2c`, one event with several occurrences can trigger an ability several times. Scryfall's ruling on Blood Artist says the same: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

So if 6 creatures died, you get 6 triggers. You choose a target player for each one, so you can split them however you like.
citations: rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities"
rule 603.10: "The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures."
rule 603.2c: "However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences."
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer:
Yes, your buddy is right. After you cast **Lightning Bolt**, you get priority back, so you can cast a second Bolt right away before he gets a chance to act. Per `117.3c`, "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." `601.2i` says the same thing for casting a spell.

He only gets priority when you pass. Per `117.3d`, if you choose not to act, you pass, and "Then the next player in turn order receives priority."

This doesn't take away his chance to counter the first Bolt, though. Nothing resolves until all players pass in a row (`117.4`). When you pass, both Bolts are on the stack and he can respond to either one. The second Bolt was cast in response to the first, so it resolves first (`117.7`). After it resolves, the active player gets priority again (`117.3b`), and everyone gets another round of priority before the first Bolt resolves. So casting both at once doesn't stop him from countering them. What it does do is commit both Bolts at **Dark Confidant** before he acts. You lose the option of waiting to see whether the first one resolves.
citations: rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 601.2i: "If the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority."
rule 117.3d: "Then the next player in turn order receives priority."
rule 117.4: "If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves"
rule 117.7: "The new spell or ability will resolve first."
rule 117.3b: "The active player receives priority after a spell or ability (other than a mana ability) resolves."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
No, the creature doesn't die, as long as its toughness is back above 0 by the time the spell finishes resolving. For the two **Ragavan**s, the legend rule applies before anyone gets priority, so there is no window to respond once the second one is on the battlefield.

**Toughness 0 mid-resolution:** State-based actions (SBAs) are only checked when a player would get priority, per `704.3`. They "pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability" (`704.4`). The **Maro** ruling says the same: if toughness hits 0 and comes back up before the resolution ends, the creature isn't put into the graveyard. Keep in mind that timing and order matter. **Giant Growth**'s +3/+3 only helps if it has already resolved. If the creature's toughness is still 0 or less when the other spell finishes, it goes to the graveyard at the next check (`704.5f`).

**Legend rule:** This is an SBA too. "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners' graveyards" (`704.5j`). SBAs happen automatically and don't use the stack (`704.1`), and they're dealt with before a player would receive priority (`117.2d`). So once the second Ragavan resolves and enters, you choose which one to keep and the other goes to the graveyard, all before anyone can act. Your only chance to respond is while the second Ragavan is still a spell on the stack. Any abilities that triggered, such as Ragavan entering, still go on the stack after the SBA check (`704.3`).
citations: rule 704.3: "Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions s…"
rule 704.4: "Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability."

ruling ef32258a-d567-4fbc-ab85-8c00080f5b36/654c63e82671903c: "If Maro’s toughness goes to 0 during the announcement or resolution of a spell or ability and then goes back up above 0 before the end of that announcement or resolution, it won’t be put into your gra…"
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."
rule 704.1: "State-based actions don’t use the stack."
rule 117.2d: "State-based actions happen automatically when certain conditions are met. See rule 704. They’re dealt with before a player would receive priority."
rule 704.5f: "If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard."

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: The premise is off: Questing Beast is a 4/4 with vigilance, deathtouch and haste, and it does not have trample, so blocked by one creature it assigns all its combat damage to that blocker and nothing goes to the player (510.1c). A good answer says so. For the creature the asker describes, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer:
You can assign just 1 to the 4/4 and trample 4 over, so your opponent is wrong. One thing first: **Questing Beast** doesn't have trample on its own. Its current Oracle text is "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste" plus its other abilities, and its base size is 4/4. So this answer assumes something is making it 5/5 and giving it trample.

With trample, you have to assign lethal damage to the blockers before any excess can go to the player, per `702.19b`. Deathtouch changes what counts as lethal: per `702.2c`, "any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage". So 1 damage is lethal to the 4/4, and the other 4 can go to the defending player (or the planeswalker or battle it's attacking). You can also put more on the blocker if you want. Damage already marked on the blocker doesn't change this.

If the 4 trample damage hits an opponent, Questing Beast's last ability also triggers, dealing 4 damage to target planeswalker that player controls.
citations: rule 702.19b: "Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the player, planeswalker, or battle the creatur…"

rule 702.2c: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt."
oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"
oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Whenever Questing Beast deals combat damage to an opponent, it deals that much damage to target planeswalker that player controls."

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
1) Yes. 2) Your choice: you can put **Kenrith** into the command zone instead of your hand, or leave him in your hand. The command zone option isn't only for the graveyard or exile.

**1)** Per `903.4`, color identity counts the mana symbols in a card's mana cost *and* its rules text. Kenrith costs {4}{W}, and his abilities use {R}, {G}, {W}, {U} and {B} (for example "{4}{B}: Put target creature card from a graveyard onto the battlefield under its owner's control."). So his color identity is all five colors. **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager** is blue, black and red. His back face counts too, per `903.4d`, but it's also blue, black and red. Every color in Bolas's identity is in Kenrith's, so `903.5c` lets you run him.

**2)** **Unsummon** says "Return target creature to its owner's hand." Per `903.9b`, if your commander would go to your hand or library from anywhere, you may put it into the command zone instead. This is a replacement effect, so Kenrith never touches your hand. It's optional. If you keep him in hand, you just cast him from your hand like a normal card, and commander tax won't apply, because per `903.8` the tax only applies when you cast him from the command zone.
citations: rule 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text"
rule 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity."
rule 903.5c: "A card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck’s commander."
rule 903.9b: "If a commander would be put into its owner’s hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead."
rule 903.8: "A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game."
oracle d209b948-9afb-4fd1-a961-72c87282878c#0: "{4}{B}: Put target creature card from a graveyard onto the battlefield under its owner's control."
oracle 837182db-1bf3-4a2c-bd01-1af9d9873561#0: "Return target creature to its owner's hand."

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
No, you don't lose. The Clone's 6 damage doesn't count toward commander damage, and damage from **Fling** doesn't count either.

The loss condition in `903.10a` only covers "combat damage by the same commander." Being a commander isn't a characteristic that a copy effect can pick up. Per `903.3`, "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself." **Clone** copies Rafiq's printed characteristics (its name, abilities, power and toughness), but it isn't the card that was named commander. So it isn't a commander, and its 6 damage is just ordinary combat damage. You're still at 15 commander damage from the real **Rafiq of the Many**. Only damage the actual Rafiq deals to you in combat adds to that count, including extra hits from its exalted and double strike boosts.

Fling fails on two counts. First, `903.10a` only counts combat damage. Second, the source is Fling itself ("Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature's power to any target"), not the commander. So even if she sacrifices the real Rafiq to Fling, you lose that much life but it adds nothing to the 21 count.
citations: rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
rule 903.3: "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself."
ruling 42226b87-0746-4ebf-9fd0-108d508462af/e115f2763b5d5e7e: "Clone copies exactly what was printed on the original creature and nothing else"
oracle 24227761-b50e-4b9e-93a2-e82d053b3e3d#0: "Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature's power to any target."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer:
1) No. The mana won't last until your main phase. Per `106.4`, "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana." Mana you add during your upkeep is gone when the upkeep ends. Tap your lands in the main phase when you cast **Jace, the Mind Sculptor**.

2) Yes, you can tap lands while you're casting **Snapcaster Mage**. You don't need to float mana first, and normally you wouldn't. When you cast a spell, `601.2g` gives you a chance to activate mana abilities after the total cost is locked in and before you pay it. `605.3a` also lets you activate mana abilities "whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment." Mana abilities don't use the stack. They resolve right away (`605.3b`), so the mana is there to pay for Snapcaster. Floating mana first also works, but it's only needed for special reasons, such as when the mana has to come from something you'll lose during the casting process.
citations: rule 106.4: "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana."

rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."
rule 605.3a: "A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment"
rule 605.3b: "An activated mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated."

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer:
Your opponent lost **3** life for Tim and **2** for Goyf. Goyf's current 5/6 doesn't matter.

**Dark Confidant** says "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value." Mana value is the total mana in the card's mana cost, regardless of color (`202.3`). Power and toughness play no part in it.

**Prodigal Sorcerer** costs {2}{U}, so its mana value is 3.

**Tarmogoyf** costs {1}{G}, so its mana value is 2. Its ability only sets its power and toughness ("Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards..."). It never changes the mana cost, so Goyf's size doesn't affect how much life Bob costs you.
citations: rule 202.3: "The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color."
oracle 2068185c-1b50-47d0-aa3f-bf505d199428#0: "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."
